title: Relative clauses 2
note: THE comma rule, and the single biggest Czech interference target at B1: Czech puts a comma before every relative clause, so students write *The man, who lives next door, is a doctor where the clause is defining and takes none. Contrast pack with b1_relative_clauses (defining + omission), which plays immediately before. Second rule: no THAT in a non-defining clause. Thickened 10 -> 25 items 2026-09-04 (agent loop): 15 new, split about evenly between defining (no commas) and non-defining (commas + who/which, never that), plus three items whose answer is `nothing` at all. Rules applied this pass: A4 all six cleared - Czech really does say `ten muz, ktery ...` for a defining clause, so the demonstrative went into the cz where the noun is definite, and the two that could not take one were rewritten (near the centre -> which they bought last year; on the second floor -> which has no windows); F3 Moravia dropped. C11: `nothing` was the answer to three items and appeared nowhere in the intro - it now has a card (When the word can be nothing). D1: the 15 new items each carry an explanation naming their own noun and clause, after a first pass that shared two strings across 13 of them. · C57 recap card (You already know — Vztažné věty 1) added as card 1; the three `nothing` items are now Quiz-only (`type: false`) — James's standing answer: the chip is the teaching point, nobody types "nothing" into a gap.

cards.title: Two kinds of relative clause
points: If you still know who is meant, it needs **commas**.

rows: **defining**
says WHICH one
no commas
**non-defining**
adds extra information
commas

examples.en: The man **who** lives next door is a doctor.

examples.cz: Můj bratr, který bydlí v Brně.

cards.title: You already know
points: A relative clause sits **right after** the noun it describes.
Drop the word only when a **new subject** follows it.

table.caption: Relative clauses 1
rows: the man **who** called
the book **which** I bought
the man **that** called
the book **that** I bought
— *(a verb follows: keep it)*
the book I bought *(dropped)*

examples.en: The man **who** called is my boss.
examples.cz: Ten muž, který volal, je můj šéf.

cards.title: Czech commas are not English commas
points: Czech marks every relative clause with commas. English marks only the extra ones.

rows: Muž**,** který bydlí vedle**,** je doktor.
The man who lives next door is a doctor.
Kniha**,** kterou jsem četl**,** byla dobrá.
The book I read was good.
Můj bratr**,** který bydlí v Brně…
My brother**,** who lives in Brno…

cards.title: Which one is it?
points: The commas change the meaning. They are not there to make the sentence look nicer.

rows: My sister who lives in Prague is a nurse.
I have more than one sister
My sister, who lives in Prague, is a nurse.
I have one sister

cards.title: No that in the extra kind
points: **that** works only in the defining kind, where there are no commas.

rows: ~~My brother, that lives in Brno…~~
My brother, **who** lives in Brno…
~~Prague, that is the capital…~~
Prague, **which** is the capital…

cards.title: When the word can be nothing
cards.title_cz: Když tam vztažné slovo být nemusí
points: If the relative word is the **object**, you can use **nothing** at all.
It still says which one, so there are still no commas.

rows: The book **that** I read was good.
The book I read was good.
The man **who** I met was nice.
The man I met was nice.
The letter **which** I sent arrived.
The letter I sent arrived.

cards.title: Common mistakes
points: No commas when the clause says **which** one.

rows: ~~The man, who lives next door, is a doctor.~~
The man **who** lives next door is a doctor.
~~My brother, that lives in Brno, is a doctor.~~
My brother, **who** lives in Brno, is a doctor.
~~Prague, that is the capital, is beautiful.~~
Prague, **which** is the capital, is beautiful.
~~The book, I read, was good.~~
The book I read was good.

items.en: The man who lives next door is a doctor.
items.cz: Ten muž, který bydlí vedle, je doktor.
items.gap: The man ____ lives next door is a doctor. (who / , who)
accepts: The man who lives next door is a doctor.
items.wrong: The man, who lives next door, is a doctor.
items.explanation: This clause tells you **which** man, so it is defining — no commas in English.
items.explanation_cz: Tahle věta říká, **který** muž to je, takže je určující — v angličtině bez čárek.

items.en: My brother, who lives in Brno, is a doctor.
items.cz: Můj bratr, který bydlí v Brně, je doktor.
items.gap: My brother, ____ lives in Brno, is a doctor. (who / that)
accepts: My brother, who lives in Brno, is a doctor.
items.explanation: Extra information about one known person, so commas and **who**, never that.
items.explanation_cz: Doplňující informace o jednom známém člověku, takže čárky a **who**, nikdy that.

items.en: Prague, which is our capital, has over a million people.
items.cz: Praha, která je naše hlavní město, má přes milion obyvatel.
items.gap: Prague, ____ is our capital, has over a million people. (which / that)
accepts: Prague, which is our capital, has over a million people.
items.wrong: Prague, that is our capital, has over a million people.
items.explanation: A non-defining clause about a thing takes **which**, not that.
items.explanation_cz: Doplňující věta o věci má **which**, ne that.

items.en: The book I read last week was very good.
items.cz: Ta kniha, kterou jsem četl minulý týden, byla moc dobrá.
items.gap: The book ____ I read last week was very good. (nothing / , which)
accepts: The book I read last week was very good.
items.wrong: The book, I read last week, was very good.
items.explanation: Defining and the pronoun is the object, so it can drop out — and there are no commas.
items.explanation_cz: Určující věta a zájmeno je předmět, takže může vypadnout — a čárky nejsou.

items.en: My sister, who is a nurse, works in Ostrava.
items.cz: Moje sestra, která je zdravotní sestra, pracuje v Ostravě.
items.gap: My sister, ____ is a nurse, works in Ostrava. (who / that)
accepts: My sister, who is a nurse, works in Ostrava.
items.explanation: One sister, so the clause is extra: commas and **who**.
items.explanation_cz: Jedna sestra, takže je ta věta doplňující: čárky a **who**.

items.en: The woman who called you is waiting outside.
items.cz: Ta žena, která ti volala, čeká venku.
items.gap: The woman ____ called you is waiting outside. (who / , who)
accepts: The woman who called you is waiting outside.
items.wrong: The woman, who called you, is waiting outside.
items.explanation: It identifies **which** woman, so no commas.
items.explanation_cz: Určuje, **která** žena to je, takže bez čárek.

items.en: Brno, which is a big city, has a lot of students.
items.cz: Brno, které je velké město, má hodně studentů.
items.gap: Brno, ____ is a big city, has a lot of students. (which / that)
accepts: Brno, which is a big city, has a lot of students.
items.explanation: A place name is already identified, so the clause is extra: **which** + commas.
items.explanation_cz: Jméno města už je určené, takže je věta doplňující: **which** + čárky.
items.wrong: Brno, that is a big city, has a lot of students.

items.en: The train that leaves at six is always full.
items.cz: Ten vlak, který odjíždí v šest, je vždycky plný.
items.gap: The train ____ leaves at six is always full. (that / , which)
accepts: The train that leaves at six is always full.
items.wrong: The train, that leaves at six, is always full.
items.explanation: It says **which** train, so it is defining — **that** is fine and there are no commas.
items.explanation_cz: Říká, **který** vlak, takže je určující — **that** je v pořádku a čárky nejsou.

items.en: My car, which I bought last year, has already broken down.
items.cz: Moje auto, které jsem koupil loni, se už porouchalo.
items.gap: My car, ____ I bought last year, has already broken down. (which / that)
accepts: My car, which I bought last year, has already broken down.
items.explanation: **my car** is already identified, so the clause is extra: **which** + commas.
items.explanation_cz: **my car** je už určené, takže je věta doplňující: **which** + čárky.

items.en: The teacher who helped me was very kind.
items.cz: Ten učitel, který mi pomohl, byl moc milý.
items.gap: The teacher ____ helped me was very kind. (who / , who)
accepts: The teacher who helped me was very kind.
items.wrong: The teacher, who helped me, was very kind.
items.explanation: **who helped me** says which teacher, so the sentence runs straight through with no commas.
items.explanation_cz: **who helped me** říká, který učitel, takže věta běží bez čárek.

items.en: The film that we saw yesterday was very long.
items.cz: Ten film, který jsme včera viděli, byl moc dlouhý.
items.gap: The film ____ we saw yesterday was very long. (that / , which)
accepts: The film that we saw yesterday was very long.
items.wrong: The film, that we saw yesterday, was very long.
items.explanation: **that we saw yesterday** says which film, so it takes no commas.
items.explanation_cz: **that we saw yesterday** říká, který film, takže žádné čárky.

items.en: The email that arrived this morning was from my boss.
items.cz: Ten e-mail, který přišel dnes ráno, byl od šéfa.
items.gap: The email ____ arrived this morning was from my boss. (that / , which)
accepts: The email that arrived this morning was from my boss.
items.wrong: The email, that arrived this morning, was from my boss.
items.explanation: Which email? The one that arrived this morning — defining, so no commas.
items.explanation_cz: Který e-mail? Ten, co přišel ráno — určující věta, takže bez čárek.

items.en: The woman who works in the shop is my neighbour.
items.cz: Ta žena, která pracuje v obchodě, je moje sousedka.
items.gap: The woman ____ works in the shop is my neighbour. (who / , who)
accepts: The woman who works in the shop is my neighbour.
items.wrong: The woman, who works in the shop, is my neighbour.
items.explanation: **who works in the shop** picks the woman out of all women. No commas.
items.explanation_cz: **who works in the shop** vybere tu ženu ze všech žen. Žádné čárky.

items.en: The man I met yesterday works with my brother.
items.cz: Ten muž, kterého jsem včera potkal, pracuje s mým bratrem.
items.gap: The man ____ I met yesterday works with my brother. (nothing / , who)
accepts: The man I met yesterday works with my brother.
items.wrong: The man, I met yesterday, works with my brother.
items.explanation: The relative word is left out because it is the object of *met* — and the clause is still defining, so still no commas.
items.explanation_cz: Vztažné slovo je vynechané, protože je předmětem k *met* — a věta je pořád určující, takže pořád bez čárek.

items.en: The bus that goes to the station is always late.
items.cz: Ten autobus, který jede na nádraží, má vždycky zpoždění.
items.gap: The bus ____ goes to the station is always late. (that / , which)
accepts: The bus that goes to the station is always late.
items.wrong: The bus, that goes to the station, is always late.
items.explanation: Not any bus — **the one that goes to the station**. Defining, no commas.
items.explanation_cz: Ne jakýkoli autobus — **ten, který jede na nádraží**. Určující, bez čárek.

items.en: The letter I sent last week arrived today.
items.cz: Ten dopis, který jsem poslal minulý týden, dnes přišel.
items.gap: The letter ____ I sent last week arrived today. (nothing / , which)
accepts: The letter I sent last week arrived today.
items.wrong: The letter, I sent last week, arrived today.
items.explanation: Nothing goes in front of *I sent*: the relative word is the object and can be dropped. Commas would make it a different sentence.
items.explanation_cz: Před *I sent* nepatří nic: vztažné slovo je předmět a dá se vynechat. Čárky by z toho udělaly jinou větu.

items.en: My mother, who is seventy, still works.
items.cz: Moje máma, které je sedmdesát, pořád pracuje.
items.gap: My mother, ____ is seventy, still works. (who / that)
accepts: My mother, who is seventy, still works.
items.wrong: My mother, that is seventy, still works.
items.explanation: You have one mother, so **who is seventy** is extra information: commas, and **who**, never that.
items.explanation_cz: Máma je jen jedna, takže **who is seventy** je doplňující informace: čárky a **who**, nikdy that.

items.en: My best friend, who lives in Ostrava, is coming tomorrow.
items.cz: Můj nejlepší kamarád, který bydlí v Ostravě, přijede zítra.
items.gap: My best friend, ____ lives in Ostrava, is coming tomorrow. (who / that)
accepts: My best friend, who lives in Ostrava, is coming tomorrow.
items.wrong: My best friend, that lives in Ostrava, is coming tomorrow.
items.explanation: *My best friend* already names the person, so the clause only adds detail — commas, and **who**.
items.explanation_cz: *My best friend* už tu osobu určuje, takže věta jen doplňuje — čárky a **who**.

items.en: This book, which I bought in Prague, is about Czech history.
items.cz: Tahle kniha, kterou jsem koupil v Praze, je o českých dějinách.
items.gap: This book, ____ I bought in Prague, is about Czech history. (which / that)
accepts: This book, which I bought in Prague, is about Czech history.
items.wrong: This book, that I bought in Prague, is about Czech history.
items.explanation: *This book* is already identified by **this**, so the clause is extra: commas and **which**.
items.explanation_cz: *This book* je určená slovem **this**, takže věta je doplňující: čárky a **which**.

items.en: Their new flat, which they bought last year, is very small.
items.cz: Jejich nový byt, který loni koupili, je moc malý.
items.gap: Their new flat, ____ they bought last year, is very small. (which / that)
accepts: Their new flat, which they bought last year, is very small.
items.wrong: Their new flat, that they bought last year, is very small.
items.explanation: They have one new flat, so when they bought it is extra information — **which**, not that.
items.explanation_cz: Nový byt mají jeden, takže kdy ho koupili je doplňující informace — **which**, ne that.

items.en: My phone, which I bought in June, is already broken.
items.cz: Můj telefon, který jsem koupil v červnu, je už rozbitý.
items.gap: My phone, ____ I bought in June, is already broken. (which / that)
accepts: My phone, which I bought in June, is already broken.
items.wrong: My phone, that I bought in June, is already broken.
items.explanation: *My phone* is one phone, so the clause adds a detail: commas, and **which** — *that* cannot follow a comma.
items.explanation_cz: *My phone* je jeden telefon, takže věta doplňuje detail: čárky a **which** — *that* po čárce stát nemůže.

items.en: The girl who works with me is from Poland.
items.cz: Ta holka, která se mnou pracuje, je z Polska.
items.gap: The girl ____ works with me is from Poland. (who / , who)
accepts: The girl who works with me is from Poland.
items.wrong: The girl, who works with me, is from Poland.
items.explanation: **who works with me** says which girl, so no commas — even though Czech puts two in.
items.explanation_cz: **who works with me** říká, která holka, takže žádné čárky — i když čeština dvě dává.

items.en: My sister, who I see every week, lives in Brno.
items.cz: Moje sestra, kterou vidím každý týden, bydlí v Brně.
items.gap: My sister, ____ I see every week, lives in Brno. (who / that)
accepts: My sister, who I see every week, lives in Brno.
items.wrong: My sister, that I see every week, lives in Brno.
items.explanation: One sister, so the clause is extra: commas, and **who** even though it is the object here.
items.explanation_cz: Jedna sestra, takže věta je doplňující: čárky a **who**, i když je tu předmětem.

items.en: The hotel that we stayed in was very cheap.
items.cz: Ten hotel, ve kterém jsme bydleli, byl moc levný.
items.gap: The hotel ____ we stayed in was very cheap. (that / , which)
accepts: The hotel that we stayed in was very cheap.
items.wrong: The hotel, that we stayed in, was very cheap.
items.explanation: **that we stayed in** tells you which hotel. Defining clauses take no commas.
items.explanation_cz: **that we stayed in** říká, který hotel. Určující věty nemají čárky.

items.en: Our office, which has no windows, is always cold.
items.cz: Naše kancelář, která nemá okna, je pořád studená.
items.gap: Our office, ____ has no windows, is always cold. (which / that)
accepts: Our office, which has no windows, is always cold.
items.wrong: Our office, that has no windows, is always cold.
items.explanation: We have one office, so the windows are extra information — commas and **which**.
items.explanation_cz: Kancelář máme jednu, takže okna jsou doplňující informace — čárky a **which**.
